newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hamas debates strategy after Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Hamas debates strategy after Hebron.

text.p: By accepting a post in Yasser Arafat's cabinet a Hebron cleric has revived a debate among Islamists about whether they should join government or work in opposition to bring about politic reform.
Some Islamists and political analysts said Talal Sider's appointment as Minister of Sports and Youth in Arafat's cabinet highlighted divisions and confusion within the Islamic movement.
Others said his move to the Palestinian Authority was part of a trend among groups such as Hamas and Islamic Jihad away from militancy to politics.

"Sider's appointment has revived the debate over changing political systems from within. It is a major step towards transforming Hamas into a political movement," political analyst Khalil Shikaki told Reuters.

Hamas, the strongest Islamic fundmentalist group in the West Bank and Gaza, views the self-rule deal for these areas that Arafat signed with Israel in 1993 as a sell-out. Hamas leaders outside Palestinian lands have never wavered in their opposition but those inside are debating how to live with the reality of Arafat and his 20,000-strong police force.

"Hamas is in a state of confusion and Sider's move was a cry for normalcy and to end the state of limbo and indecision. The confusion could allow other hesistant Hamas leaders to join the Authority," Shikaki said.
Although he was among 415 Hamas and Islamic Jihad supporters banished to Lebanon by Israel in 1992, Sider said he was only a senior figure in the broad Islamic movement and did not belong to Hamas.
Yet, Sider's move astonished many in the Moslem fundamentalist Hamas group, which nearly wrecked Israeli-PLO peace moves with suicide bombings.
Although his links to Hamas are murky, many top Hamas figures said they opposed his appointment and expected the group to sever links with him.
Hamas issued a leaflet distancing itself from Sider and rejecting his move. But it stopped short of attacking him personally.

"We view Sheikh Sider's decision of accepting the appointment as a personal initiative that is rejected by us," the Hamas leaflet said. "We reiterate that Hamas has no representatives in the self-rule Authority."
Arafat has sought to change Hamas into a political movement since he returned to Gaza in 1994, using both the carrot and stick. Analysts said he has succeeded in dividing and weakening the group.
Sider insisted that his appointment would not alter his opposition to the peace accords and Arafat's policies.
"Of course I believe in opposition from within the political system, and if anyone wants to join me, they are welcome," Sider told Reuters.

Tayeb Abdel-Rahim, the PLO's main negotiator with Hamas, said: "Sider's appointment strengthens the moderate trend within the Islamic movement. It's a major development and is a step towards transforming Hamas into a political group."
Some local Hamas leaders openly differed with the more powerful leadership in exile over the group's future course and its relations with Arafat's Authority.

Imad al-Fallouji, once a Hamas leader in Gaza, was expelled last year even before he joined the Palestinian Authority as communications minister. But others stayed on and are even gaining ground within the group.
Adnan Maswadeh, a senior Islamic figure in Hebron said he was against Sider's move but urged Hamas to respect the decision.

"I advise the movement (Hamas) to refrain from taking a hardline position against Sheikh Talal," Maswadeh said. "But we believe it is wrong now to see the position of those wishing to participate in the Authority strengthened."
Other Hamas officials disagreed but said they were not prepared to defy Hamas's decisions now for fear of dividing the group.

"There weren't many violaters in the movement, but we are seeing more of them now because the movement lacks a clear political strategy," said a leading Islamist, who declined to be identified. "And if confusion remains, there could be splits."
